chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Said from Al-Hasan from Zur'ah from Samaan from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): In

the man who buys a slave while he is fugitive (abiq) from his master, he (peace be upon him) said: 'It is not valid for him except that he buys another thing with him and says: I buy from you this thing and your slave for such and such. If he is unable to get the slave, then what he paid is for what he bought from him.'

key_terms.آبِق: Fugitive slave who has run away from his master

ai.seo_question: What is the legal ruling for buying a fugitive slave in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This narration from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) provides a practical legal mechanism to mitigate *gharar* (uncertainty) in transactions involving a fugitive slave (*al-abiq*), ensuring the buyer’s capital is protected. By bundling the purchase with another item, the transaction remains valid even if the slave escapes, reflecting the Shia emphasis on preserving economic rights through precise contractual conditions. This ruling highlights the juristic balance between commercial flexibility and risk management in classical Islamic law.
